paragraphs.source_en:
Here is a reference list for the names of the intervals. (Note: Two half steps equals one whole step.)

Simple Intervals Compound Intervals 0 steps = perfect unison (identical pitches) octave + minor 2nd = minor 9th 1/2 step = minor 2nd Octave + major 2nd = major 9th 1 whole step = major 2nd octave + minor 3rd = augmented 9th 1 1/2 steps = minor 3rd octave + major 3rd = perfect 10th 2 whole steps = major 3rd octave + perfect 4th = perfect 11th 2 1/2 steps = perfect 4th octave + diminished 5th = diminished 12th/augmented 11th 3 whole steps = diminished 5th or tritone (augmented 4th} octave + perfect 5th = perfect 12th 3 1/2 steps = perfect 5th octave + minor 6th = minor 13th/augmented 12th 4 whole steps = minor 6th (augmented 5th) octave + major 6th = major 13th 4 1/2 steps = major 6th (diminished 7th) octave + minor 7th = minor 14th 5 whole steps = minor 7th octave + major 7th = major 14th 5 1/2 steps = major 7th two octaves = perfect 15th

6 whole steps = octave

INTERVAL FAMILIES

Intervals are grouped into two categories, or families: The major/minor family (2nds, 3rds, 6ths, and 7ths), and the perfect family (unisons, 4ths, Sths, and octaves). When a major interval is lowered by a half step it is called minor. When a perfect interval is lowered by a half step it is called diminished. When a major or perfect interval is raised a half step it is called augmented, (See. Fig. 2
